analysis.one_liner: Restores employer liability for workplace harassment by any boss who directs an employee's daily work.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have expanded employer liability for workplace harassment, was referred to four House committees and never received a hearing or vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would undo a 2013 Supreme Court decision (Vance v. Ball State University) that narrowed who counts as a 'supervisor' in harassment lawsuits. Under current law, an employer is automatically liable when the harasser can hire, fire, or discipline the victim — but not when the harasser merely controls the victim's daily work, like assigning shifts or schedules. The bill would make employers liable for harassment by anyone authorized to direct an employee's daily work activities, or when employer negligence allowed a hostile environment to continue. It would apply across federal anti-discrimination laws covering sex, race, age, disability, and genetic information discrimination, and would also cover congressional employees under the Congressional Accountability Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are harassed by shift leads, crew chiefs, and others who control their day-to-day work but cannot formally hire or fire them — a group concentrated in retail, restaurants, health care, housekeeping, and personal care, where low-wage workers and women are heavily represented [S3]. The bill's findings cite EEOC data showing sex discrimination made up nearly a third of charges in 2016 and that low-wage workers, women, and people of color are especially vulnerable to harassment by people with day-to-day authority over them [S3]. It would also extend the same standard to federal employees and to congressional employees [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers harassed by shift leads and crew bosses

how_it_helps.text: Makes employers liable for harassment by anyone they authorize to direct an employee's daily work activities, reversing the Vance v. Ball State University limitation to harassers who can take tangible employment actions like hiring and firing [S2].

Applies the new standard across Title VII, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Rehabilitation Act, Section 1981, GINA, and federal-employee statutes, so protections cover sex, race, age, disability, and genetic-information harassment [S2].
Extends the same liability standard to congressional employing offices under the Congressional Accountability Act, closing a gap for Capitol Hill workers [S3].

Restores strict employer liability when a supervisor's harassment results in tangible employment actions, and employer liability where employer negligence allowed a hostile environment to form or continue [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers — particularly businesses with large low-wage and hourly workforces — would face broader vicarious liability in harassment lawsuits, increasing their litigation exposure and settlement costs. Business groups have historically opposed expanding harassment liability standards on these grounds (general knowledge).

drawbacks.text: Expanding vicarious liability to anyone who directs daily work could significantly increase employers' legal exposure and litigation costs, including for conduct by lower-level employees with modest authority [S3].
The bill applies retroactively to all claims pending on or after enactment, which could reopen settled expectations in ongoing cases [S3].

Defining 'directs daily work activities' may be litigated heavily, since many workplaces have fluid reporting lines, and Section 12 preserves all existing employer defenses, which could blunt the bill's practical effect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is a real one: workers in industries where harassers control schedules and daily tasks but cannot formally fire people currently lose lawsuits on a technicality, while employers gain a defense that insulates them from that conduct. The bill addresses this by restoring the pre-2013 functional standard, while keeping the existing Faragher/Ellerth defenses available through Section 12 [S2, S3]. The main cost is greater litigation exposure for employers, especially small businesses with informal hierarchies. The design is a targeted reversal of one Supreme Court holding rather than a broad rewrite, which limits both its benefit and its disruption.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced and later sent to a Judiciary subcommittee, but no committee ever held a hearing or markup and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced October 26, 2017 by Rep. DeLauro with nine original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1].

Referred to four committees — Education and the Workforce, House Administration, Judiciary, and Oversight and Government Reform — a multi-committee referral that requires each panel to act before the bill can move [S5].
On November 17, 2017, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a companion Senate action, and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers benefit from the bill's death: the narrower Vance v. Ball State University liability standard remains in force, so businesses can still avoid liability for harassment by supervisors who direct daily work but cannot hire or fire. Workers in retail, restaurants, health care, and housekeeping who face such harassment remain without the remedy the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers; workers left without the fix

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore the pre-2013 harassment liability standard across federal anti-discrimination laws.

for.name: 20 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 20 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support.

against.name: House committee chairs (Education and the Workforce, House Administration, Judiciary, Oversight)
against.role: Chairs of the four committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the 115th Congress; the record shows referral and subcommittee referral only, with no further action [S5].

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House schedule in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Allowed the bill to die in committee without a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors plus the sponsor were Democrats; no Republicans sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and it received no action under Republican committee control [S4].

industries.industry: Employers with low-wage hourly workforces (retail, restaurants, health care, housekeeping, personal care)
industries.note: These employers would face vicarious liability for harassment by shift leads and crew chiefs who direct daily work, increasing settlement and litigation costs. Their gain from the bill's death is workers' continued lack of recourse against such harassment [S3].

industries.industry: Employment defense bar and businesses generally
industries.note: The narrower Vance standard that the bill would have repealed remains law, preserving a defense that limits employer liability to harassers with hiring-and-firing authority. Business groups generally opposed restoring the broader standard (general knowledge).
